Banyana Banyana: Champions of Africa

By: Diana Lucas | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Finally Banyana Banyana in their second successive final have become Africa’s women soccer champions, winning the 2022 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations at their sixth attempt. The long standing curse finally broken.

Two ways to do this story, one is to do a celebratory piece on these champions for this Sunday. They return to South Africa on Tuesday.

Profiling two player like Hildah Magaia and Rosella Ayaane and their inspirational coach Desiree Ellis – who last week won her third coach of the year award.

This win is sits starkly against Bafana Bafana’s own poor record since winning the CAF Cup in 1996.

We could also do something more in depth, the stories of some of the players and Desiree’s own story is hugely inspirational. The rise of woman’s soccer is evident by the record-breaking crowds at the European Championships in England.

Script:


When Banyana Banyana landed at OR Tambo after their historic victory at the Women’s African Cup of Nations … South Africans took a break from the state of the nation to celebrate our African Queens 

Two successive Olympics 2012 and 2016, now two successive world cups and two successive finals and finally the gold medal.

Claire: Have you come down from the high that you were on when you got back after winning?
Desiree: Not at all, not at all. When I think about it I just have this broad smile on my face… 
Banyana Banyana have consistently reached the final since the Women’s African Cup of Nations or WAFCON began in 1995. But in previous years the trophy remained just out of reach …
Team coach Desiree Ellis knew this time was going to be different.
I made sure that I had some tissues in my pocket, because I am a very emotional person, I wear my heart on my sleeve…
Knowing they had substantial support at home, gave Desiree and the team that extra confidence boost to bring the trophy home.
Desiree: We knew when we walked out in that final that they might have 50,000 but we’ve got almost 60million behind us. So we were not in any way phased and not afraid to take them on.
Banyana Banyana won 2-1 against Morocco in their own backyard. Rabat, … crowning their unbeaten record at this tournament…

Still in awe about it still get goose bumps, and first time winning it so failure after failure equals success for me. 
Janine van Wyk –  one of two Banyana Banyana captains – is South Africa’s most-capped soccer player.
I couldn’t stop taking that smile off my face my cheeks started hurting It was just amazing to see support and support shown to women’s football something we strived for for many years…
Worldwide support for Women’s football has exploded
In London’s Wembley stadium at the end of July the UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 final between England and Germany broke all attendance records for any European Championship final, indicating that things indeed are changing.

A crowd of over 87 000 fans packed the stadium… as an English national soccer team won its first major championships since 1966… Globally we’re celebrating the dawn of a new era for female football.
 
After the euphoria has died down, the dust has settled and players returned to their clubs in distant lands, what is the long term impact on women’s football in South Africa?

I don’t think we realise the magnitude of what we have done/ I think we have changed the way people think not just about women’s football but also women in sport, 
Women like Desiree have fought tooth and nail to be taken seriously at club and national levels. For Desiree it started in the 70s.
Back in the day it wasn’t the norm for a girl to play football I was constantly told that I wanted to be a boy all I wanted to do was play the sport that I loved and I think what helped me was my parents support. 
 
 
That support helped her overcome the prejudice she encountered.
 
It didn’t matter what teachers thought at school or what the neighbours said when I was playing with the boys . It didn’t matter at all even when they said they will send me to school bare feet. because my school shoes were always broken but my father was my biggest supporter. I am where I am because of him never good enough tried to be better and better.
 
Football was in my DNA from a very young age. I started playing with the boys at the age of 6. It was very rare for girls to play football back then I received a lot of negative comments from the boys, from the boy’s parents the oppositions, from my own team mates at times when they didn’t want a girl on their team.

For Janine even finding a women’s team was a battle, the first team she played for was in KwaThema township, Springs.

I was this white girl going into an African community and a lot of people couldn’t believe this white family coming into their community wanting to play football.…
Determination is what set these women apart.  Desiree joined Banyana Banyana in the 90’s, and quickly rose to the captaincy. But it was a different time, and it wasn’t until 2009 that the pendulum started shifting.


Thirteen years ago there were barriers for women to advance in football. SASOL wanted to play a role…. And they were in for the long haul, the companies decision to invest was based on their belief in inclusion.
When you’re making investment long term with young women and girls through sport you have got to stay the long haul
Charlotte Mokoena, a leading force behind SASOLS partnership with Banyana Banyana.
Claire: How do you measure the return on investment in something like this? 
Charlotte: This is not traditional brand management, where you are looking at only the commercial outcome of it. It was not the investment intent. The investment intent was much bigger than that it was intent to make sure we created a platform for young women to advance through sports.
In 2018 Desiree was appointed as head coach for Banyana Banyana, to lead the team through the WAFCON tournament. 
From the word go I surrounded myself with experts I am still a baby in coaching.

What a professional and what a leader she is really dedicated to make sure she brings out the best in the individual and the team
But applause and flying the flag are not enough… The success of Desiree and her team has again highlighted an issue some prefer not to talk about: pay disparity.
Despite Bafana Bafana’s DISAPPOINTING record since winning AFCON in 1996, the men earn - on average - 10 times more than their female counterparts.. 
Banyana Banyana's success has forced soccer bosses to commit to equal pay, for equal work.
Claire: What difference will it make in the player’s life to get that equal pay?
Desiree: She doesn’t have to work 9 to five and then go to club training she doesn’t have to depend on anyone else she can take care of herself and her family. Can you Imagine if they were able do this full time they would then be able to concentrate solely on football and not worry about where the next meal is coming from or worry about are they going to get money to pay the rent.
There is no full time professional women’s football league in South Africa, forcing players to make tough decisions.
It's a struggle to make a living out of football making a career out of football in South Africa and many of us actually go abroad to actually to get rewarded for what we do at the end of the day. It’s amazing to see so many represent South Africa in different countries abroad.

Recognising the challenges facing young football players Janine started the JVW Football Club in 2012.

Janine: I identified so many young girls playing at boys at school level and there was no opportunity for them and I wanted to see and be the change of that so I wanted to just create a platform for these girls to express full potential and ability in the sport that they love. 
14-year old Tatiana Correia started playing football when she was three years old and joined the club about a year ago with big dreams for her future.
 
I love soccer so to become a professional that would be amazing I mean playing in the WAFCON, the Euros, FIFA World Cup that’s my dream.
Over the 10 years we have had players represent the junior, senior and national team so far and we are incredibly proud of what we have created and also just to see the growth in the woman’s game over the past years has been incredible.
17 year-old Cimone Sauls who has been with the JVW Football Club for 6 years and this year was called up to the Banyana Banyana squad trials

I didn’t make the finals but hopefully next year I will make the final squad I am still young I have a lot ahead of me so It just pumps me up you know knowing that I have already trained with those players been with those players. 
For young soccer stars, the future looks promising…  But a future only likely to deliver on its promise IF the game’s top brass deliver on theirs.
We are seeing that there is a wave of change and you heard me when I was speaking I did not say W Afcon I said Afcon. I did not say W Fifa I just said Fifa that’s how it needs to recognized. That’s what its about that we have to be able to advance equity in sports.
There’s definitely no going back and that is why I am so excited that we have qualified for the FIFAS world cup once again no matter who plays every single game is going to be sold out and its going to be an amazing atmosphere and 2023 will be the new evolution of women’s football globally

Now we have that gold medal that no one can take away from us… history makers that no one can take away from us and I think that’s what the players need to remember for all the hard work they have put in
